props.title: The Apartment
props.initialSlug: Insurance clerk lends apartment for office affairs

sections.content: The Apartment masterfully blends corporate satire with romantic melancholy. Billy Wilder crafts a perfect storm of comedy and tragedy through Jack Lemmon's C.C. Baxter, a low-level insurance worker who loans his apartment to cheating executives. The film's genius lies in how it tackles adultery and workplace exploitation while maintaining a light touch, much like Wilder's earlier Some Like It Hot (1959). The Manhattan office scenes prefigure later workplace critiques like Working Girl (1988) and Office Space (1999), but with a darker emotional core.

sections.content: Wilder's sharp critique of corporate America feels startlingly modern. The endless rows of desks in the Consolidated Life office directly influenced Brazil (1985) and Being John Malkovich (1999). Lemmon's performance as the eager-to-please Baxter established a template for the corporate everyman that echoes through films like Save the Tiger (1973) and American Beauty (1999), where professional success comes at a devastating personal cost.

Shirley MacLaine's Fran Kubelik brings extraordinary depth to what could have been a simple love interest role. Her complicated relationship with Fred MacMurray's callous executive Sheldrake anticipated the complex power dynamics explored in 9 to 5 (1980) and Secretary (2002). The film's Christmas Eve sequence remains one of cinema's most powerful depictions of loneliness in the city, influencing works like Lost in Translation (2003). sections.content: The Apartment's influence extends beyond romantic comedy into biting corporate satires. Films like Network (1976) and Wall Street (1987) build on its critique of business ethics, while modern works like Up in the Air (2009) and The Big Short (2015) echo its ability to find humanity within systemic corruption. Wilder's genius was making audiences laugh while exposing the rot beneath corporate America's polished surface.
